real-gases-s1.title: PV/nRT for four gases at 350 K
real-gases-s1.text: For each gas, PV/nRT at 350 K, calculated from reference equations of state fitted to measured data. An ideal gas would give exactly 1.

real-gases-s2.title: Ammonia in a steel cylinder
real-gases-s2.text: A student fills a rigid steel cylinder with ammonia and measures its pressure.

items.q: Which gas never falls below PV/nRT = 1 at any pressure shown?
options: He
Ar
CH₄
CO₂

why.correct: Helium’s curve starts at 1 and only rises. Its atoms attract each other so weakly that only the volume effect shows, and it grows with pressure.
options: Right: above 1 throughout.
Ar dips just below 1 at moderate pressure before rising above it near 200 atm.
CH₄ dips below 1 at moderate pressure.
CO₂ falls well below 1.

items.q: Why does CO₂ show the largest dip below PV/nRT = 1?
options: CO₂ molecules attract each other most strongly, lowering the pressure most.
CO₂ molecules are the smallest of the four, so they slip between the others and lower the pressure.
CO₂ molecules take up the most volume, which lowers the measured pressure below the ideal value.
CO₂ molecules move fastest at 350 K, so they collide with the walls less often than the others do.

why.correct: A value below 1 means the pressure is lower than ideal, which is the effect of attractions. CO₂ has the most electrons (22) and polar bonds, so its attractions are the strongest of the four.
options: Right: below 1 points to attractions.
CO₂ is one of the larger molecules here, not the smallest.
Particle volume makes PV/nRT larger than 1, not smaller.
CO₂ is the heaviest gas here, so it moves slowest at 350 K.

items.q: Above about 200 atm, Ar’s PV/nRT rises above 1, and it keeps rising. Which explanation fits?
options: The molecules' own volume becomes a real share of the container, so real V exceeds ideal V.
At very high pressure the attractions between Ar atoms become repulsions, which push the walls outward.
At very high pressure the Ar atoms are squeezed smaller, so each one pushes harder on the walls.
At very high pressure the temperature of the gas rises, so the molecules hit the walls harder.

why.correct: When the atoms are packed close, the space they cannot enter (their own volume) is no longer negligible. Real V is larger than ideal V, so PV/nRT exceeds 1.
options: Right: particle volume dominates at very high pressure.
The effect is from the particles' own volume, not from attractions turning into repulsions at a distance.
Atoms are not squeezed smaller; their fixed size is exactly why the volume effect appears.
The data are all at 350 K, so the temperature is constant.

items.q: At 1 atm, by about what percent does CO₂ differ from ideal behavior?
options: About 90%
About 34%
About 16%
About 0.3%

why.correct: At 1 atm, PV/nRT for CO₂ is 0.997, which is 0.3% below 1. That is why the ideal gas law works well at ordinary pressures.
options: No gas in the graph deviates that much at any pressure shown.
That is the deviation at 100 atm, not at 1 atm.
That is the deviation at 50 atm, not at 1 atm.
Right: a small deviation at low pressure.

items.q: The CO₂ measurements are repeated at 500 K instead of 350 K. How would the CO₂ curve most likely change?
options: Closer to 1, because faster molecules are less affected by attractions.
Farther below 1, because hot molecules attract each other more strongly than cold ones.
Unchanged, because PV/nRT already includes T and so cancels out the change.
Far above 1, because hot molecules swell and take up more volume than cold ones.

why.correct: At higher temperature molecules move faster, so the brief tug of a neighbor changes their motion less. Gases behave more ideally at high temperature.
options: Right: high temperature favors ideal behavior.
The attractions themselves do not grow with temperature; their effect on fast molecules shrinks.
T in the denominator does not remove the effect of attractions on the measured P.
Molecules do not swell when heated.

items.q: What pressure does the ideal gas law predict for the ammonia?

mistakes.why: Value: you used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). With liters and atm, use R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K).

items.q: Calculate PV/nRT for the ammonia from the measured pressure.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the ideal pressure by the measured one. PV/nRT puts the measured P on top.

why.correct: PV/nRT = P(measured) / P(ideal) = 62.5 atm / 73.854 atm = 0.8463, which is 0.846.

items.q: Which claim about the ammonia is best supported by the data?
options: Attractions dominate: hydrogen bonds between NH₃ molecules lower the pressure.
Particle volume dominates: the NH₃ molecules fill so much of the cylinder that the pressure is lower than the ideal value.
Ammonia behaves ideally, because the measured pressure is within a few atm of the ideal pressure.
Some NH₃ molecules decompose at 450 K, so fewer particles are present and the pressure is lower.

why.correct: The measured pressure is 15% below ideal, the signature of attractions. NH₃ molecules hydrogen-bond (H on N to an N lone pair), strong attractions for a gas.
options: Right: a lower-than-ideal pressure points to attractions.
Particle volume raises PV/nRT above 1; here it is below 1.
A 15% shortfall is a large deviation, not ideal behavior.
Ammonia is stable at 450 K; the evidence fits attractions, not decomposition.

items.q: The same 2.000 mol of gas at 450.0 K is put in a 100.0 L tank instead. How would PV/nRT for the ammonia compare with the value in the 1.000 L cylinder?
options: Much closer to 1, because the molecules are far apart.
Farther from 1, because the molecules have more room to build up speed between collisions.
The same, because PV/nRT depends on the kind of gas and not on the conditions.
Farther below 1, because a larger tank lets more hydrogen bonds form between the molecules.

why.correct: In 100 L the pressure is about 0.74 atm. The molecules are far apart, so they rarely feel each other's attractions and their volume is negligible: nearly ideal.
options: Right: low pressure favors ideal behavior.
Speed depends on temperature, which is unchanged.
Deviations depend strongly on pressure and temperature.
Molecules far apart have fewer neighbors, so attractions matter less.

items.q: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
options: High temperature and low pressure
Low temperature and high pressure
Low temperature and low pressure
High temperature and high pressure

why.correct: Fast particles (high T) are barely affected by attractions, and particles far apart (low P) have negligible volume and few neighbors.
options: Right: fast, far-apart particles.
These conditions make both deviations largest, near condensation.
Low temperature makes attractions matter.
High pressure makes particle volume and attractions matter.

items.q: At the same temperature and pressure, which gas deviates most from ideal behavior?
options: SO₂ (polar, 32 electrons)
Ne (nonpolar, 10 electrons)
H₂ (nonpolar, 2 electrons)
He (nonpolar, 2 electrons)

why.correct: Deviations from attractions grow with intermolecular forces. SO₂ is polar with many electrons, so it attracts its neighbors most strongly.
options: Right: polar and polarizable.
Ne has few electrons and weak dispersion forces.
H₂ has the weakest attractions of almost any gas.
He is the most nearly ideal real gas.

items.q: Which statement explains why a real gas at moderate pressure usually has a lower pressure than the ideal gas law predicts?
options: Attractions between particles reduce how hard they strike the walls.
The particles take up space, so they have less room and hit the walls more often.
The collisions between particles are perfectly elastic, so energy is lost to the walls.
The particles are moving more slowly than the kinetic molecular theory predicts.

why.correct: A particle near the wall is pulled back by its neighbors, so the force on the wall is less than for an ideal gas.
options: Right: neighbors pull particles back from the wall.
Particle volume raises the pressure (or volume) above ideal; it does not lower it.
Elastic collisions lose no energy; this is an ideal-gas assumption, not a deviation.
At a given temperature the average kinetic energy is set; the attractions are what differ.

items.q: Which changes make a sample of CO₂ behave LESS ideally? Select all that apply.
options: Cooling it toward its condensation temperature
Compressing it to a much higher pressure
Heating it at constant volume
Expanding it into a much larger container

why.correct: Cooling slows the molecules so attractions matter more; compressing crowds them so attractions and molecular volume matter more. Heating and expanding do the opposite.
options: Right: slow molecules feel attractions more.
Right: crowded molecules feel attractions, and their volume counts.
Heating makes the gas more ideal.
Expanding lowers the pressure and makes the gas more ideal.

items.q: At 300 K, PV/nRT for He is 1.005 at 10 atm. A student concludes that helium atoms repel each other. Which response is best?
options: Above 1 comes from the atoms' own volume; helium's attractions are too weak to offset it.
The student is right: a value above 1 means the particles repel, so they push harder on the walls.
A value above 1 means helium has strong attractions, which makes its measured pressure higher.
The value is within error of 1, so helium is exactly ideal and no explanation is needed.

why.correct: Two departures compete: attractions lower PV/nRT, and particle volume raises it. Helium attracts so weakly that only the volume effect remains, giving a value slightly above 1.
options: Right: volume, not repulsion, raises the value.
The volume effect raises the value; long-range repulsion is not needed to explain it.
Attractions push PV/nRT below 1, not above.
A steady deviation that grows with pressure is real, not error; it has a physical cause.

items.q: A real gas has PV/nRT = 0.92 under certain conditions. If its pressure at those conditions is measured as 46.0 atm, what pressure would an ideal gas have?
options: 42.3 atm
46.0 atm
50.0 atm
92.0 atm

why.correct: PV/nRT = P(real)/P(ideal) at the same n, V and T, so P(ideal) = 46.0 / 0.92 = 50.0 atm. The real gas pushes less because of attractions.
options: This multiplies by 0.92 instead of dividing.
The ratio is not 1, so the pressures differ.
This multiplies by 2 for no reason.

items.q: At 450 K and 50 atm, which gas would have PV/nRT farthest below 1? Select all that apply.
options: NH₃ (polar, hydrogen-bonding)
He (2 electrons)
Ne (10 electrons)
H₂ (2 electrons)

why.correct: Attractions push PV/nRT below 1, and NH₃ attracts its neighbors by hydrogen bonds, far more strongly than the small, barely polarizable He, Ne or H₂.
options: Right: the strongest attractions.
He has the weakest attractions of any gas; it sits slightly above 1.
Ne's dispersion forces are weak.
H₂'s dispersion forces are very weak.
